title: A House for David: God's Covenant Promise
summary: Settled in his palace, David wants to build a house for the ark of God, and Nathan the prophet at first agrees. That night God answers through Nathan that David will not build him a house; instead God will build David a house, a dynasty, and establish the throne of his offspring forever. David goes in, sits before the LORD, and answers with a prayer of astonished gratitude.
story:
This is one of the high points of the whole Old Testament. David, anointed as a shepherd boy (1 Samuel 16), has been made king over all Israel, has taken Jerusalem and built a palace there (chapter 5), and has brought the ark of God into the city with dancing (chapter 6). Now, at rest from his enemies, he turns to what seems the obvious next step: a temple. God overturns the plan and makes a promise instead.

The promise to David stands alongside the promise to Abraham in Genesis 12 and the covenant at Sinai as one of the load-bearing beams of the Bible's story. It narrows the blessing promised to Abraham's offspring to a royal line and attaches to it the hope of a permanent kingdom. The chapters that follow test it at once: David's wars (chapter 8), his kindness to Saul's grandson (chapter 9), and then his adultery and murder (chapters 11 and 12), after which his own house is torn by violence. The promise survives David's sins and his sons' rebellions. From here on Israel's kings are measured against David, the psalms sing his covenant (Psalms 89 and 132), the prophets look for a son of David to come when the dynasty falls, and the New Testament opens by calling Jesus “the son of David” (Matthew 1:1). David himself, at the end of his life, calls it an everlasting covenant (2 Samuel 23:5).
historical:
David's reign is usually dated to about 1010 to 970 BC, though the exact figures depend on how the chronology of the kings is reconstructed. The chapter places the promise after God has given David rest from his enemies, although the victories themselves are listed in chapter 8, so the writer arranges events by theme rather than strict order. The same scene appears, with small differences, in 1 Chronicles 17. The Chronicler omits the note of rest and later explains that David could not build the temple because he had shed much blood (1 Chronicles 22:8), while 1 Kings 5:3 says that he was prevented by constant wars; Samuel itself gives neither reason and grounds the refusal simply in God's will. Nathan appears here for the first time. He will confront David after Bathsheba (chapter 12) and help put Solomon on the throne (1 Kings 1), and 1 Chronicles 29:29 mentions records of Nathan the prophet among the sources for David's reign.

The historical David has been much debated. Some archaeologists, notably Israel Finkelstein and Neil Asher Silberman (David and Solomon, 2006), argue that tenth-century Judah was a thinly settled highland chiefdom and that the Bible's picture of a kingdom was magnified later. Others point to sites such as Khirbet Qeiyafa, a fortified town above the Elah Valley excavated from 2007 by Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor and dated to the early tenth century, as evidence of organized rule in Judah in David's time. The dynasty itself is attested outside the Bible. An Aramaic victory inscription found at Tel Dan in northern Israel, its main fragment discovered in 1993 and two more in 1994, refers to a king of the house of David (bytdwd). It was most likely set up by Hazael of Damascus in the second half of the ninth century BC, more than a century after David's death, and most scholars take it as the earliest known reference to David's dynasty by name. André Lemaire proposed in 1994 that the Moabite Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) also mentions the house of David in line 31, a reading others dispute. Assyrian scribes likewise called the northern kingdom Bit-Humri, the house of Omri, naming a kingdom by its founding dynasty just as this chapter does.

The building of a temple was, across the ancient Near East, a royal act that needed a god's approval. The cylinders of Gudea, ruler of Lagash around 2100 BC, describe how he rebuilt the temple of Ningirsu after a dream, omens, and repeated confirmation from the god. The Sumerian poem known as the Curse of Agade blames the fall of Naram-Sin's city on his violation of Enlil's temple after the omens refused him. Victor Hurowitz (I Have Built You an Exalted House, 1992) gathered these building accounts and showed how the biblical accounts of Solomon's temple share their pattern. Against this background David's plan is natural, and God's refusal is striking.

The promise was already read as a messianic hope before Jesus. Among the Dead Sea Scrolls, the text known as 4QFlorilegium (4Q174), copied in the late first century BC, quotes verses 10 to 14 and applies the son to whom God will be a father to the Branch of David, who will arise with the Interpreter of the Law in the last days, joining the passage with Amos 9:11 through the verb raise up. The Psalms of Solomon, written after the Roman general Pompey took Jerusalem in 63 BC, pray in Psalm 17 for God to raise up the son of David as king. The fifteenth blessing of the daily Amidah, the standing prayer of the synagogue in its Babylonian form, still asks God to make the shoot of David his servant flourish.
cultural:
In the ancient Near East, kings built temples for their gods, and the building project was proof that the god had blessed the king and a claim that the god had chosen him. A victorious ruler living in a cedar palace while his god lived in a tent would look, by the standards of the day, like a king neglecting his patron. Cedar was the prestige timber of the region, brought down from Lebanon, and Hiram of Tyre had supplied it for David's palace (5:11). David's wish is pious and entirely conventional. God's reply cuts against the convention: he has never asked for a house, he has always moved with his people in a tent (the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary built in the wilderness), and he does not need a king to secure his dwelling. The word for his dwelling, mishkan, comes from a verb meaning to dwell or settle, and it pictures a presence among the people rather than a residence to be guarded.

The oracle calls David a shepherd taken from the flock (verses 7 and 8), and shepherd was an ancient royal title; Hammurabi of Babylon calls himself the shepherd of his people in the prologue to his laws. In Israel the image carries responsibility as much as honor, and later prophets judge kings as shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34). The title nagid, ruler or leader (verse 8), is used of Saul and David as men designated by God (1 Samuel 9:16; 13:14), stressing appointment over royal status.

The promise itself uses the language of adoption. “I will be his Father, and he will be My son” (verse 14) is the kind of language ancient kings used for their relationship to a patron god. In Egypt the pharaoh was called the son of the sun god Re, a claim of divine birth; in Israel the king becomes God's son by covenant, not by nature, and Psalm 2:7 gives the formula of the day he is installed. The discipline clause fits the image: a son is corrected, not disowned (Proverbs 3:11-12). Moshe Weinfeld (Journal of the American Oriental Society, 1970) compared the promise to royal grants in which a great king rewarded a loyal servant with land or a dynasty that passed to his heirs even if they sinned. Gary Knoppers (same journal, 1996) argued that the structure and language of the grants differ too much for a real parallel. The chapter never uses the word covenant (a binding, sworn relationship), but later texts call it that (2 Samuel 23:5; Psalm 89:3; 132:11-12). Finally, David sits before the LORD to pray (verse 18), an unusual posture; the Talmud later records a rule that no one sat in the temple court except kings of the house of David (b. Yoma 25a), a rule that reflects this scene.
literary:
The chapter turns on a pun. The Hebrew word bayit means a house, a palace, a temple, and a dynasty, and the chapter uses all four, fifteen times in all. David lives in a house of cedar (verse 2) and wants to build God a house (verse 5); God answers that “He Himself will establish a house for you” (verse 11), meaning a royal line, and that David's son “will build a house for My Name” (verse 13), meaning the temple Solomon will build. David's prayer takes up the word again and again, ending with the house of your servant blessed forever (verse 29). The play turns the natural religious order upside down: God will build for David before David's son builds for God.

The oracle (verses 4 to 17) moves from the past (what God has done for Israel and for David) through the near future (a son and a temple) to the far future (a throne forever). It opens with a question that carries its answer (are you the one to build me a house?) and a review of history (verses 6 to 9), then turns on the announcement of verse 11. David's prayer (verses 18 to 29) mirrors it. It moves from humility (who am I, O Lord GOD?) through praise of God's uniqueness and of Israel's redemption from Egypt (verses 22 to 24) to bold petition introduced by and now (verses 25 and 28). It calls David your servant ten times and addresses God as Lord GOD (Adonai YHWH) seven times, a form of address rare elsewhere in Samuel. David asks for nothing God has not already promised.

The chapter also stands at a structural point in the larger history that runs from Deuteronomy to Kings. Martin Noth (1943) identified speeches placed at the turning points of that history (Joshua 23, 1 Samuel 12, 1 Kings 8), and Dennis McCarthy (Journal of Biblical Literature, 1965) argued that 2 Samuel 7 belongs among them. Frank Moore Cross (Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic, 1973) traced two themes through Kings: the sin of Jeroboam, which doomed the northern kingdom, and God's faithfulness to David, which kept a lamp burning in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36; 15:4; 2 Kings 8:19). Both rest on this chapter. So does the tension that runs through the rest of the Old Testament between the unconditional language here (verses 15 and 16) and the conditions attached elsewhere (1 Kings 2:4; 9:4-7; Psalm 132:12).

outline.t: David proposes a temple, and Nathan agrees
God has never asked for a house
What God has done for David and Israel
The promise of a son, a house, and a throne forever
David's prayer: who am I, and who is like You
David asks God to do as he has promised

doctrines.note: The Davidic covenant is initiated by God and rests on his promise, not David's achievement. It takes up the promise to Abraham (a great name, a place for the people, an heir from his own body) and narrows it to a royal line through whom God will rule his people. Discipline is possible within it; withdrawal of God's loyal love is not (verses 14 and 15).

The promise of a descendant whose throne God will establish forever is the root of Israel's hope for a coming anointed king, the Messiah. Later prophets build directly on it (Isaiah 9:6-7; 11:1-5; Jeremiah 23:5-6; Ezekiel 34:23-24), it was read messianically at Qumran (4Q174), and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as the son of David who reigns forever (Luke 1:32-33).

God's presence with Israel was never tied to a building. He moved with his people in a tent, and the temple will be a house for his Name, built at his initiative by David's son. Solomon's prayer draws the lesson that heaven cannot contain God (1 Kings 8:27), and the New Testament speaks of a house built of people (Ephesians 2:19-22).

The king rules God's people on God's behalf: Israel remains my people throughout the oracle, and the parallel in Chronicles speaks of God's own house and kingdom (1 Chronicles 17:14). The kingdom of God in Scripture has a Davidic shape, which is why the Gospels announce it through a son of David.

David's prayer models asking God to keep his word. He does not bargain or boast; he marvels at the gift, praises the Giver, rehearses what God has said, and asks him to do it, so that God's name will be magnified. The promise itself is what gives him courage to pray (verse 27).

words.note: Bayit, house. One of the commonest nouns in the Hebrew Bible, it occurs about 2,000 times, and its range covers a building, a palace, a temple, a household, and a dynasty. The standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) list all these senses, and this chapter uses every one of them. Here in verse 11 it means a royal line. David offers to build God a house; God promises to build David one. The reversal is the theology of the chapter in a single word: grace comes before service.

Chesed, loving devotion, steadfast love. It occurs about 250 times and names loyal, covenant-keeping love that goes beyond what is strictly owed, often shown by the stronger party to the weaker. God promises that his chesed will never be removed from David's son as it was from Saul (verse 15). Isaiah 55:3 later speaks of the faithful mercies promised to David (the plural of this word), and Paul applies that verse to the resurrection of Jesus (Acts 13:34).

Olam, forever, a long age. It occurs about 440 times and eight times in this chapter, in the promise and in the prayer. The word can mean a very long or indefinite time rather than endless time in a philosophical sense, but here it is set against Saul's short-lived line, and later readers took it at full strength. That is why the fall of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC raised such hard questions (Psalm 89:38-51) and why the promise kept Israel hoping.

Zera, seed, offspring. It occurs about 230 times, usually of plant seed or of descendants, and is singular in form whether it means one child or a whole line. The BSB renders it descendant in verse 12. The same word carries the promise to the woman's offspring (Genesis 3:15) and to Abraham's (Genesis 12:7; 15:5), and the phrase from your own body repeats Genesis 15:4, so the Davidic promise joins a chain of promises about a coming seed. Paul argues from its singular form in Galatians 3:16.

Kun, to be firm, and in the forms used here to establish or make secure. It occurs about 220 times and five times in this chapter, of the son's kingdom (verse 12), his throne (verses 13 and 16), God's people Israel (verse 24), and David's house (verse 26). The verb is often used of God establishing the earth and his throne (Psalm 93:1-2), so the promise ties David's dynasty to the stability of God's own rule.

Aman, to be firm, reliable, and in the passive to be made sure or to endure. The verb occurs about a hundred times and is the root of amen and of emunah, faithfulness. In verse 16 David's house ‘will be made sure’ before God. Abigail had predicted that God would make David a sure house (1 Samuel 25:28), and Isaiah plays on the root when he warns David's house that if they do not stand firm in faith they will not stand at all (Isaiah 7:9).

Nagid, ruler, leader. It occurs about 44 times and is used especially of Saul, David, and Solomon as rulers designated by God (1 Samuel 9:16; 13:14; 25:30; 1 Kings 1:35), and later of other officials. Unlike melekh, king, it stresses appointment by a higher authority. In verse 8 God reminds David that he took him from the flock to be nagid over my people Israel: David's authority is delegated, and the people remain God's.

Eved, servant, slave. The noun occurs about 800 times and ranges from a slave to a royal minister to a worshiper. As a title for someone in God's service it is an honor, given to Abraham, Moses, and Caleb; God calls David my servant in verses 5 and 8. David uses it of himself ten times in his prayer, and the word frames the relationship: the king whom God calls son speaks of himself as servant. The title lives on in the prophets' hope for my servant David (Ezekiel 34:23-24).

christ:
The New Testament reads this chapter as fulfilled in Jesus. The angel tells Mary that God will give her son “the throne of His father David” and that “His kingdom will never end” (Luke 1:32-33), taking up throne, house, and forever from verses 13 to 16. Paul opens Romans by describing God's Son as “a descendant of David according to the flesh” (Romans 1:3) and declared Son of God in power by the resurrection, joining the two titles of verse 14. Peter at Pentecost says that David knew God “had promised him on oath that He would place one of his descendants on his throne” (Acts 2:30) and spoke of the resurrection of the Christ, and Paul at Pisidian Antioch ties God's raising up of David's seed to the raising of Jesus (Acts 13:22-23, 34). Hebrews 1:5 quotes verse 14, “I will be His Father, and He will be My Son”, of Christ, alongside Psalm 2:7.

The immediate referent of verses 12 to 15 is Solomon, who builds the temple (1 Kings 5:5; 8:20) and whose wrongdoing brings discipline; the New Testament does not deny that. It sees in Jesus the son of David in whom the promise's forever finally holds. The clause about discipline for wrongdoing fits Solomon and the later kings, not Jesus, and Hebrews quotes only the first half of the verse, a reminder that the promise is fulfilled across a history rather than in a single prediction. Augustine (City of God 17.8-9) argued that the promise was not fulfilled in Solomon, whose kingdom was limited and divided after him, and applied the discipline clause to Christ's members rather than to Christ himself.

The temple thread runs the same way. Jesus spoke of the temple of his body (John 2:19-21), and the New Testament describes the church as a house built of living stones (1 Peter 2:5; Ephesians 2:19-22), so that the son of David builds God a house not of cedar but of people. Jesus himself raised the question of how the Messiah can be both David's son and David's Lord (Mark 12:35-37, citing Psalm 110). Paul adapts the father-son promise to all God's people as sons and daughters (2 Corinthians 6:18), and the Bible's last chapter calls Jesus the root and offspring of David (Revelation 22:16). The link between this chapter and Jesus is not an allegory imposed later but the development of a promise the Old Testament itself kept open when the dynasty fell.
interpretation:
The chapter's reinterpretation begins inside the Bible. Chronicles retells it with Solomon idealized, omitting the discipline clause and speaking of God's own house and kingdom (1 Chronicles 17:13-14). Psalm 89 recites the promise at length and then laments that God has renounced it, and Psalm 132 sings it with its condition. Isaiah 55:3 extends the faithful mercies of David to the whole people, and the prophets of the exile speak of a shoot from Jesse's stump and a righteous branch for David (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5). After the exile Haggai hoped for Zerubbabel, David's descendant, as God's signet ring (Haggai 2:23). At Qumran, 4Q174 read verses 10 to 14 of the Branch of David of the last days, and the Psalms of Solomon (Psalm 17) prayed for a son of David to purge Jerusalem of foreigners. The synagogue's daily prayer asks for the flourishing of the shoot of David, and Maimonides, codifying Jewish messianic hope (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11:4), defined the Messiah as a king from the house of David who would rebuild the temple and gather the exiles, criteria that shaped Jewish rejection of Christian claims about Jesus.

Christian interpreters read the chapter from the start through Luke 1, Acts 2 and 13, and Hebrews 1. Augustine devoted chapters of City of God (book 17, chapters 8 and 9) to Nathan's oracle and Psalm 89, arguing that the promise looked past Solomon to Christ, who builds a house of believers, and reading the iniquity clause, as Psalm 89 does with its his children, of the members of Christ's body. The Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 1 to 11 and 16 on the Fourth Sunday of Advent in Year B with the annunciation of Luke 1:26-38, and verses 1 to 14a in summer of the same year.

Modern study has asked about the chapter's origin and genre. Siegfried Herrmann (1953) compared it to the Egyptian royal novella, a court genre in which a king receives a divine word, often about a temple. Martin Noth, Dennis McCarthy (1965), and Frank Moore Cross (1973) placed it at the center of the history running from Joshua to Kings, and commentators such as P. Kyle McCarter (II Samuel, Anchor Bible, 1984) have traced older and later layers in it. Moshe Weinfeld (1970) and Gary Knoppers (1996) debated its relation to royal grants, and Jon Levenson (Sinai and Zion, 1985) explored how the covenant with David relates to the covenant at Sinai. Walter Kaiser (1974) read the obscure phrase of verse 19 as the charter for humanity, the promise that God's blessing for all people would come through David's line.
text:
Several differences between English Bibles come from the Hebrew text itself, often visible when Samuel is compared with its parallel in 1 Chronicles 17. In verse 7 Samuel reads ‘the tribes of Israel’ and Chronicles ‘the judges of Israel’; the two Hebrew words differ by one letter, and many translations follow Chronicles because the verse speaks of leaders God appointed to shepherd his people. In verse 16 the Masoretic Text reads that David's house will endure ‘before you’ (that is, before David); the Septuagint and some Hebrew manuscripts read ‘before Me’, which the BSB follows. In verse 21 Samuel has ‘for the sake of your word’ and Chronicles ‘for the sake of your servant’, two words that look alike in unpointed Hebrew. Verse 23 is rough in Hebrew, with a plural verb after Elohim that could be read ‘gods went’ and a phrase ‘for your land’ where Chronicles reads ‘to drive out nations’; the BSB and most modern versions follow Chronicles.

Other differences are translation choices. The last clause of verse 19, literally ‘and this is the torah of man’, is rendered ‘Is this your custom with man?’ (BSB), ‘this is instruction for mankind’ (ESV), or ‘is this the manner of man?’ (KJV), and the parallel in 1 Chronicles 17:17 is equally difficult. In verses 9 to 11 the verb forms can be read as future promises (most versions) or partly as a description of what God has already done, which affects whether the rest promised to Israel is present or still to come. Chronicles omits the clause about discipline in verse 14 and reads ‘I will set him over My house and My kingdom forever’ in its version of verse 16. Hebrew and English verse numbers are the same in this chapter.

teach.big: God refuses to let David build him a house and instead promises to build David a house forever, so that the kingdom rests on God's grace and faithfulness, fulfilled in Jesus, the son of David.

outline.t: A good desire to serve God can still be our plan rather than his, and even a true prophet can speak too soon.
God does not need what we offer him; he has always chosen to dwell with his people on his own terms.
Before God asks anything of David, he recalls what he has done: taking a shepherd from the flock, going with him, and giving rest.
God's promise rests on his loyal love, which disciplines the son but never abandons him, and it reaches forever.
The right response to grace is astonished humility and praise of the God who has no equal and who redeemed a people for himself.
Bold prayer grows out of God's own promises and aims at the honor of his name.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats verses 1 to 3 as a lesson in waiting for God's specific permission before any good project, which makes the text a manual for decision-making; the point is the reversal of verse 11, not a method of guidance. The second reads the chapter as a promise of success for a believer's own family, career, or ministry, borrowing forever for private ambitions. The promise is made to David's royal line for the sake of God's people and fulfilled in Christ; believers share it through him, not by claiming its words for their own houses.

Teachers should also avoid two opposite errors about Solomon and Christ. One skips Solomon and reads verses 12 to 15 as if they spoke only of Jesus, which makes the discipline clause impossible. The other stops with Solomon and treats the New Testament's reading as arbitrary, though the Old Testament itself kept the promise open after the dynasty fell. Finally, the chapter should not be taught as a proof that God endorses a particular nation's rulers or political order. Its king is under God, its people remain God's people, and the kingdom it promises is the one Jesus announced.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses gently on people whose good plans God has closed, such as a ministry that did not happen or a calling they could not pursue. David's disappointment is answered not with a lecture but with a larger gift, and teachers can say so without promising that every closed door will be explained. The discipline clause may press on those who fear that their failures have put them outside God's care, or who have known a father whose discipline was harsh. Verse 15 speaks of discipline that never becomes abandonment, and for those whose earthly fathers failed them the promise ‘I will be his Father’ can be taught as a picture of a faithfulness they have not known from anyone else.

hard.q: God promised David's throne would last forever, yet Judah's monarchy ended in 586 BC. Did the promise fail?
hard.a:
The objection is voiced first by Scripture itself. Psalm 89 recites the promise at length and then accuses God: “You have renounced the covenant with Your servant and sullied his crown in the dust” (Psalm 89:39). After Babylon destroyed Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BC, no descendant of David ruled again; Zerubbabel governed under Persia, and the hopes Haggai placed in him faded. Skeptical readers draw the obvious conclusion that the promise was a piece of royal propaganda that history disproved. Many critical scholars add that the chapter itself shows signs of revision: Frank Moore Cross (1973) argued for a first edition of the history under Josiah, confident in the Davidic promise, and a second in exile that added conditions to explain the dynasty's fall, so that the unconditional and conditional strands reflect different periods.

Several responses have been given. Some readers stress that the promise always had a conditional element for individual kings (verse 14; 1 Kings 2:4; Psalm 132:12) while the line itself was guaranteed (verse 15; Psalm 89:30-37), so that judgment on particular kings and even the loss of the throne did not cancel it. Jon Levenson (Sinai and Zion, 1985) showed how Israel held the unconditional promise to David together with the conditional covenant at Sinai. The prophets kept the promise alive through the exile, speaking of a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1) and a righteous branch for David (Jeremiah 23:5), a hope that implies the tree has been cut down. Jewish tradition continued to pray for the restoration of David's kingdom in the Amidah and looks for a messianic son of David still to come. Christians confess that the promise is kept in Jesus, descended from David, raised from the dead, and reigning, so that the forever throne is his (Luke 1:32-33; Acts 2:30-36). Across these readings, the chapter's claim is that God's commitment to David's house outlasts the failures of David's sons; how that commitment is fulfilled is where Jewish and Christian readers part.

hard.q: The promise in verses 12 to 15 plainly concerns Solomon. Is it legitimate to read it as a promise about Jesus?
hard.a:
The objection is strong. The text speaks of a son who will come from David's body after his death, build the temple, and be disciplined when he does wrong, and 1 Kings says Solomon built the temple as the fulfillment of these words (1 Kings 5:5; 8:20). Jewish interpreters have long pointed out that the clause about wrongdoing cannot describe a sinless Messiah and that Jesus neither built the temple nor restored David's political kingdom; Maimonides' criteria for the Messiah (Laws of Kings 11:4), a Davidic king who rebuilds the temple and gathers the exiles, were framed partly in that argument. Many critical scholars read the oracle as dynastic legitimation for Solomon's line, not as prediction at all.

Christian interpreters answer in several ways. The New Testament does not deny the Solomonic reference; Hebrews 1:5 quotes only the first half of verse 14, and the Chronicler had already idealized Solomon and dropped the discipline clause. The promise's forever reaches far beyond Solomon, whose kingdom split at his death, and Augustine (City of God 17.8) argued on that ground that it was not fulfilled in him. Jewish readers before Christianity also read the passage of a coming son of David (4Q174; Psalms of Solomon 17), so a messianic reading was not a Christian invention. Most Christian scholars describe the promise as fulfilled in stages or as typology: God's word to David's line is realized partly in Solomon and fully in the son who reigns forever. Some add, with Augustine, that the discipline clause applies to Christ's people rather than to Christ. Whether the passage is best called prediction, typology, or developing promise is a second-order question among Christians; the confession that Jesus is the Christ, the son of David, is the church's first-order faith, and Jewish readers' disagreement with it should be stated fairly.

observe: What did David notice about his own house and the ark's dwelling in verse 2, and what did Nathan first tell him?
List the promises God makes to David in verses 9 to 16. Which are about David himself, which about Israel, and which about his offspring?
How does David describe himself and how does he describe God in his prayer (verses 18 to 29)?
interpret: Why do you think God refused David's offer and made a promise instead? What does the play on the word house teach about who builds for whom?
How can verse 14 promise both discipline and a love that will never be removed? What does the contrast with Saul add?
Why did Israel keep hoping in this promise after the monarchy ended, and how does the New Testament read it?
apply: When has God redirected a sincere plan of yours? How might David's response help you receive a no from God?
David asks, “Who am I, O Lord GOD, and what is my house?” When has an undeserved gift left you with a similar question?
David prays by asking God to do what he has already promised. Which of God's promises could shape the way you pray this week?
